university: The University of Texas at Austin

documents.unit: Office of the Executive Vice President and Provost, Office of Academic Technology
documents.title: AI for Teaching & Learning Toolkit: Policy & Recommendations
tiers: permitted / prohibited / partially permitted (instructor chooses per course)
documents.summary: The Provost's Office of Academic Technology toolkit page requires every syllabus to carry a course AI policy and leaves the choice of permitted, prohibited or partially permitted to each course. It adds university-level rules on disclosure recommendations, requiring AI, detection software and human review of AI used in grading, and links to other offices.
documents.stance_why: The page sets no single university stance: it says 'Every syllabus must include a course AI policy that designates whether AI is permitted, prohibited, or partially permitted', handing the decision to instructors, so the stance is delegates.

units.why: The page opens by saying the university 'has issued guidance on many aspects of generative AI', framing the toolkit as an institution-level framework; I chose P56 (framework/scope) because it states purpose and scope, not a rule.
units.anchor: has issued guidance on many aspects of generative AI and other AI technologies on campus

units.why: The FAQ says 'UT does not endorse AI-detection software and holds no central contract for it', so the university gives instructors no sanctioned detector; closest type is P39 (do not rely on detectors), though it states non-endorsement rather than unreliability.
units.anchor: UT does not endorse AI-detection software and holds no central contract for it.
units.fit_note: States non-endorsement and no central contract, not that detectors are unreliable.

units.why: The toolkit points to the process for reporting 'academic misconduct like unauthorized use of AI', which classes unauthorized AI use as misconduct handled by Student Affairs; P36 fits, with P81 not chosen because no procedural steps are given here.
units.anchor: academic misconduct like unauthorized use of AI
units.policy: Unauthorized use of AI is academic misconduct, handled through the Division of Student Affairs misconduct-reporting process.

units.why: The library entry says it gives guidance on 'disclosing AI use, avoiding plagiarism and hallucinated sources, and citing generative AI', a pointer to disclosure and citation guidance; P24 fits best although it is only a pointer and also touches verification (P31).
units.anchor: disclosing AI use, avoiding plagiarism and
units.policy: University Libraries provides guidance for students and instructors on disclosing AI use, avoiding plagiarism and hallucinated sources, and citing generative AI in APA, MLA and Chicago style.
units.fit_note: A pointer to guidance; also mentions avoiding hallucinated sources (P31) and citation styles (P25).

units.why: The Acceptable Use entry directs readers to 'uses of AI that are allowable and prohibited under University guidance and state law', a pointer on data and tool rules; P77 (comply with law and university policy) fits.
units.anchor: allowable and prohibited under University guidance and state law
units.policy: Users should become familiar with the uses of AI that are allowable and prohibited under University guidance and state law.

units.why: The Decision Matrix entry tells readers to 'understand what kinds of data can be used with which tools', a data-protection and vetted-tool pointer, so P50.
units.anchor: what kinds of data can be used with which tools
units.policy: Users should understand what kinds of data can be used with which tools (Local and Cloud Services Decision Matrix).

units.why: The graduate-education entry offers 'recommendations for departments creating and maintaining generative AI policies for graduate students', so departments are expected to write their own policies; P85 (units set own rules) fits, not P04 because it addresses departments.
units.anchor: recommendations for departments creating and maintaining generative AI policies for graduate students

units.why: The FAQ says UT Austin 'provides free access to a variety of AI tools' and 'UT Sage lets you design custom tutors', a university-provided sanctioned tool for courses; P17 fits and P51 (free access) is secondary.
units.anchor: UT Sage lets you design custom tutors that can be accessed by students in Canvas.

units.why: 'Every syllabus must include a course AI policy' is a mandatory syllabus statement for all courses, binding instructors, so P09 with must.
units.anchor: Every syllabus must include a course AI policy

units.why: The same sentence requires the policy to 'designate whether AI is permitted, prohibited, or partially permitted', leaving the choice to each course; I chose P04 (each instructor sets the rule) over P05 because the three categories are what the instructor selects, not a defined tier scheme with named levels.
units.anchor: designates whether AI is permitted, prohibited, or partially permitted, with clear conditions for use
units.policy: Each course's AI policy designates whether AI is permitted, prohibited, or partially permitted, with clear conditions for use.
units.fit_note: Also names three categories of use (P05) without defining tiers.

units.why: 'If you permit or partially permit AI, give written instructions on what is allowed and how students should disclose their use' obliges instructors to put allowed uses and disclosure expectations in writing; P09 fits (communicating in writing) though disclosure (P24) is also part.
units.anchor: give written instructions on what is allowed and how students should disclose their use
units.fit_note: Also requires telling students how to disclose AI use (P24).

units.why: The sentence points instructors to 'sample statements in Your Syllabus at UT Austin', offering templates for the required syllabus policy; P09 (syllabus statement) fits.
units.anchor: See the sample statements in
units.policy: Sample AI syllabus statements are provided in Your Syllabus at UT Austin.

units.why: Answering 'Can I require students to use a generative AI tool?' with 'Yes, if such use is essential to the assessment of course learning outcomes' lets instructors require AI under a condition; P79 fits.
units.anchor: Yes, if such use is essential to the assessment of course learning outcomes.

units.why: Where tools are recommended but not required, instructors are told to 'provide accommodations to students with reasonable objections', an equity and alternatives rule; P51 fits.
units.anchor: we suggest that instructors provide accommodations to students with reasonable objections

units.why: 'In all cases, use of AI tools should be carried out responsibly' is a general expectation on AI use in the classroom, closest to P56 as a general principle with no specific content.
units.anchor: use of AI tools should be carried out responsibly
units.fit_note: Very general principle; no specific content on what responsible use means.

units.why: 'Diligence about transparent use is a key aspect of AI fluency' explains disclosure as part of a skill students should have, so I code P44 (AI use as a professional skill) rather than P24, which is the rule itself (coded next).
units.anchor: Diligence about transparent use is a key aspect of AI fluency.

units.why: The Office 'recommends that appropriate citations and AI disclosure statements be included in significant work products', a recommendation (not a mandate) to disclose AI use with submissions; P24 with should.
units.anchor: recommends that appropriate citations and AI disclosure statements be included in significant work products

units.why: 'Check your discipline's or professional organization's style guide' defers the format of AI disclosure to disciplinary style guides; P24 is nearest, but this is about format, not tool or prompt detail (P25).
units.anchor: how to appropriately disclose AI use in your context.
units.policy: Check your discipline's or professional organization's style guide for how to appropriately disclose AI use.
units.fit_note: Defers disclosure format to the discipline's style guide; does not say what details to include.

units.why: On AI grading the FAQ says 'many reasons to think twice before automating aspects of the teaching and feedback process', discouraging but not forbidding instructor AI use in feedback; P59 (instructor use of AI) fits, with P101 used for the conditions below.
units.anchor: many reasons to think twice before automating aspects of the teaching and feedback process

units.why: 'Instructor guidance is a crucial part of the learning process' gives the reason for caution about automating feedback; it is rationale about human instruction by instructors, which no rationale type captures, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Instructor guidance is a crucial part of the learning process.
units.uncovered_note: Rationale that instructor guidance and feedback are essential to learning, offered as a reason not to automate feedback.

units.why: Citing Texas law that AI 'must not autonomously make or be a controlling factor in making consequential decisions without meaningful human review', naming grading and evaluation of academic work; P73 (humans responsible for decisions about people) is chosen over P46 because the rule covers many decisions, not only grades.
units.anchor: make or be a controlling factor in making consequential decisions without meaningful human review
units.fit_note: The listed decisions include grading, evaluation of academic work, curriculum and teaching materials, and research (P46, P59, P62).

units.why: Instructors are told to 'exercise the practice of human-in-the-loop' and 'review all output since you are solely responsible', a condition on instructor AI use in grading and similar work; P101 fits.
units.anchor: making sure that you review all output since you are solely responsible for the result

units.why: 'grading systematically with machine learning might be acceptable for some assignments' permits some automated grading, while the next clause warns generative AI is not reliably consistent; P101 (conditions for AI grading) fits.
units.anchor: grading systematically with machine learning might be acceptable for some assignments
units.policy: Grading systematically with machine learning might be acceptable for some assignments, but generative AI tools do not, by design, consistently and reliably produce the same output every time.

units.why: Instructors unsure what kind of AI an academic technology tool uses are told to 'reach out to the Office of Academic Technology', which is faculty support for understanding AI; P63 fits.
units.anchor: reach out to the Office of Academic Technology

documents.title: Acceptable Use of Generative AI Tools
documents.summary: The Information Security Office sets data and tool rules for generative AI across the university: what data may go into which tools, which tools are unapproved, and the Texas-law limit on AI making consequential decisions. It says little about coursework itself.
documents.stance_why: The page allows AI use with conditions ('may be used freely' for public data; Controlled data only with university-contracted tools) and prohibits unauthorized tools and fraudulent use, so it permits AI under conditions rather than banning or delegating.

units.why: The preamble says the guidance outlines 'acceptable practices for utilizing generative AI tools while safeguarding institutional, personal, and proprietary information', stating purpose and scope; P56 fits.
units.anchor: outlines acceptable practices for utilizing generative AI tools while safeguarding institutional, personal, and proprietary information

units.why: The preamble describes the covered tools as 'large language models (LLM), diffusion models, or generative AI applications', defining what the guidance covers; P61.
units.anchor: generative AI applications known as large language models (LLM), diffusion models, or generative AI applications

units.why: 'developed collaboratively by the Office of Legal Affairs, University Compliance Services, the Information Security Office, and the Business Contracts Office' states who made the guidance; P84.
units.anchor: developed collaboratively by the Office of Legal Affairs, University Compliance Services, the Information Security Office

units.why: 'Additional guidance may be forthcoming as circumstances evolve' says the guidance is provisional; P54.
units.anchor: Additional guidance may be forthcoming as circumstances evolve.

units.why: Public or Published data 'may be used freely with AI tools' is a permission tied to data classification; closest type is P50 (protect data, vetted tools) as the permissive side of the same data-classification rule.
units.anchor: may be used freely with AI tools
units.policy: Data that is publicly available or classified as Published university information may be used freely with AI tools.
units.fit_note: A permission for public data, the permissive side of a data-protection rule.

units.why: Controlled or Confidential data 'can be used with AI tools that are managed by the university and covered by contracts explicitly protecting university data', limiting sensitive data to vetted tools; P50.
units.anchor: can be used with AI tools that are managed by the university and covered

units.why: The contracts must ensure data is not used for training or is isolated, and 'web search functionality must be disabled', a specific technical condition on vetted tools; P50 is nearest but the web-search rule is more specific.
units.anchor: web search functionality must be disabled
units.fit_note: Adds contract conditions (no training, isolated instance) and a requirement to disable web search.

units.why: The Local and Cloud Services Decision Matrix 'provides information on AI tools and the types of university data authorized for use with each tool', i.e. the approved-tool list; P92.
units.anchor: provides information on AI tools and the types of university data authorized

units.why: 'use should be consistent with the Acceptable Use Policy' ties AI use to an existing university policy, P77.
units.anchor: use should be consistent with the
units.policy: In all cases, AI use should be consistent with the Acceptable Use Policy.

units.why: AI tools that 'lack a university contract and appropriate data-sharing controls are not approved for use with Controlled or Confidential university information', including free ChatGPT and Copilot; P92 (use approved tools) fits as the prohibition side.
units.anchor: AI tools that lack a university contract and appropriate data-sharing controls are not approved
units.fit_note: Frames the rule as what is not approved for Controlled or Confidential data rather than as a duty to use approved tools.

units.why: The list names 'AI Detection software' among tools not approved for Controlled or Confidential data, so detector use with student information is restricted; no type covers a detector-specific data rule, so P50 with a fit note.
units.anchor: free or non-UT-managed versions of AI tools like ChatGPT and Copilot, and AI Detection software
units.fit_note: Specifically places AI detection software among unapproved tools for sensitive data, which also bears on detection (P39/P40).

units.why: 'Student records subject to FERPA, health information, proprietary information' must not be used with unauthorized AI tools, a must-not data-protection rule; P50.
units.anchor: must not be used with unauthorized AI tools

units.why: Texas law 'prohibits state agencies, including UT Austin, from deploying AI intended to autonomously make or be a controlling factor in making consequential decisions without meaningful human review', listing grading, admissions, discipline and academic integrity; P73.
units.anchor: prohibits state agencies, including UT Austin, from deploying AI intended to autonomously make
units.fit_note: The list of consequential decisions includes grading, student conduct and academic integrity, admissions, hiring, and research evaluation.

units.why: 'UT Austin's CISO must review AI tools to be used for any of these purposes prior to their procurement, development, deployment, or use' requires approval before deployment; P65.
units.anchor: CISO must review AI tools to be used for any of these purposes

units.why: 'AI tools must not be used for activities that are illegal, fraudulent, or violate any state or federal laws, or UT Austin or UT System policies', a general conduct ban; P74 fits (P77 secondary).
units.anchor: AI tools must not be used for activities that are illegal, fraudulent

units.why: Accepting click-through agreements 'without delegated signature authority may result in personal responsibility for compliance with the terms and conditions of the AI tool', warning of personal liability; no type covers this.
units.anchor: may result in personal responsibility for compliance with the terms and conditions
units.uncovered_note: Warns that accepting a tool's click-through terms without signature authority can make the individual personally responsible for compliance.

units.why: 'ensure compliance with IRUSP Standard 22, which outlines requirements for vendor and third-party controls' requires vendor compliance review for external AI tools; P65.
units.anchor: ensure compliance with IRUSP Standard 22

units.why: The page points to the 'UT.AI Hub for solutions, training, and community conversations', offering training and resources; P70.
units.anchor: Explore the UT.AI Hub for solutions, training, and community conversations

units.why: Users with appropriate-use questions are told to 'contact the UT Information Security Office', which names the office to ask; P80 is nearest but this is a contact point, not interpretation or enforcement authority.
units.anchor: please contact the UT Information Security Office at
units.fit_note: A contact for questions rather than a statement that the office interprets or enforces the policy.

units.why: The revision history shows 'Added Heightened Scrutiny AI to the prohibited use list to align with Texas state law', evidence that the policy is revised over time; P54.
units.anchor: Added Heightened Scrutiny AI to the prohibited use list to align with Texas state law.

notes: Coder A. Both documents are partial quality (provost page is mostly a link list with an FAQ). Only the two included university-layer documents were coded.
